q: The technician says both water tanks are full. The panel shows this. What do you do before you sign?
a: Switch the selector to tank 2 and look into both fillers yourself
o: Sign — the gauge reads the tank not in use
Ask him to top up tank 1 and sign
Note 'gauge faulty' on the form and sign
why: A gauge reads the selected tank; a quarter-full tank 1 is the first thing to see — check both tanks at the filler before signing.

q: On the side deck you find three deck caps; the lettering has worn off. Your crew is already uncoiling the pontoon hose. What do you do?
a: Have the technician identify each cap and mark it before any hose goes in
o: Try each cap — water goes in the one that gurgles
Fill the aft one; water fillers are always aft
Fill the biggest cap; the water tank is the largest
why: Water in the diesel tank or the holding tank ends the week; caps are marked WATER, DIESEL, WASTE — if they are not, mark them.

q: You are filling the water tanks at the pontoon with the marina hose. How do you do it?
a: Run the hose clear first, then fill each tank until water comes out of its vent
o: Put the hose in, go to the shop and come back in an hour
Fill only the tank the selector is on; the other fills by itself
Fill through the galley tap so the pump stays primed
why: A hose that has lain in the sun holds stale water; fill each tank until water shows at its vent, and stay with it.

q: Every tap is closed, yet the pressure pump keeps running. The technician says it is just priming. What do you do?
a: Switch the pump off and ask the base to find the leak before you leave
o: Leave it; a pump stops by itself once it finds pressure
Open a tap to let the air out and let it run on
Sign and switch it off at night to save the batteries
why: A pump that runs with the taps closed is pumping into a leak or from an empty tank — on a full tank, that water is going into the bilge.

q: Monday morning at anchor. Your crew report this. What do you do?
a: Run the engine for half an hour — the heater element only works on shore power
o: Switch on the inverter so the heater element can run
Open the hot tap and wait; the element takes an hour
Report it to the base as a broken water heater
why: The calorifier is heated by the engine's cooling water or by a 230 V element on shore power; at anchor only the engine heats it.

q: You are leaving the pontoon. The heads bowl is full of water and the pump lever is on 'wet'. What do you do?
a: Pump the bowl dry and set the lever to 'dry'
o: Leave it; the water keeps the smell down
Set the lever to 'dry' and leave the bowl full
Pump the bowl full so the seal stays wet at sea
why: A full bowl slops and can siphon when the boat heels; at sea the bowl is pumped dry and the lever left on dry.

q: A crew member reads the sign over the heads and asks whether the wipes she bought can go in. What do you answer?
a: No — only what has been eaten and a little paper; wipes go in the bin
o: Yes, if the packet says 'flushable' and you pump well
Yes, one at a time with plenty of pumping after it
Yes, in the electric heads but not in the manual one
why: Wipes do not break up; they block the pump and the holding tank, and the contract charges you for the unblocking.

q: Sunday afternoon in a bay. The crew are going ashore for lunch and the boat will be empty for three hours. This is how you leave it. What do you change?
a: Close the heads seacocks and the gas valve, and switch the pump off
o: Close the gas valve; the rest is fine for three hours
Switch the pump off; seacocks stay open to vent the heads
Close the seacocks; the pump must stay on for the fridge
why: An empty boat is left with seacocks shut, gas off at the bottle and the pressure pump off: nothing can flood or leak while nobody is aboard.

fig.title: Leaving the boat, 13:00
lines: Gas valve at the bottle: open

q: The technician shows you the holding-tank valve in this position, in the marina. What do you do?
a: Set it to 'tank' now and open it only when you are well offshore
o: Leave it; direct overboard saves pumping the tank out
Set it to 'tank' and never open it; the base pumps out
Leave it in the marina; switch to 'tank' once at sea
why: In harbour and in bays everything goes to the tank; the valve is opened only offshore, where the briefing allows discharge.

q: At check-in the holding tank reads this. The technician suggests you empty it at sea tomorrow. What do you do?
a: Ask the base to pump it out before you sign; a full tank is not an accepted boat
o: Sign and open the valve at the first bay tomorrow
Sign, and empty it over the side tonight after dark
Sign and note 'tank full' so the return check is fair
why: You take over a boat with an empty holding tank; discharging in a bay or a harbour is illegal, and the full tank is the base's job to fix.

q: The electric heads flush weakly and the bowl empties slowly. The technician says they are all like that. What do you do?
a: Write it on the check-in form and ask for it to be checked before you leave
o: Accept it; a slow flush is normal for a macerator
Sign, and use the forward heads all week
Sign; you will clear it yourself with vinegar
why: A weak flush is a blocked or tired pump that will fail mid-week; note every fault on the form and ask for the fix at the base.

fig.title: Electric heads, aft cabin
lines: Flush: a trickle, bowl empties in 30 s

q: The technician hands you this list and says the seacocks are 'all fine'. What do you ask for?
a: To be shown each one, turn it yourself, and have a bung tied beside each
o: To be shown the engine one; the others are small
To have the bungs counted in the tool bag
To have the list signed by him as checked
why: You need to know where every seacock is and that it turns; a bung tied to the fitting is found in the dark, one in a bag is not.

q: You lift the sole boards and find this. The technician says it is the fridge drain. What do you do?
a: Have it dried out and the fridge drain shown to you, then check it stays dry
o: Sponge it out yourself and sign; fresh water is harmless
Sign; the automatic pump will take it when it rises
Note 'fridge drain' on the form and sign
why: A dry bilge at check-in is your baseline: any water later is news; a fridge that drains to the bilge is a known source, but it is checked first.

q: The technician says the bilge pumping is 'automatic, you never need it'. How do you check the bilge pumps?
a: Lift the float until the pump runs, then find the handle and work the manual pump
o: Switch the electric pump to 'manual' on the panel and listen for it
Pour a bucket into the bilge and wait for the float to start it
Ask for the pumps' last service date to be written on the form
why: The float switch is tested by lifting it, the manual pump by pumping it — and its handle must be where you can find it with water over the sole.

fig.title: Bilge pumps
lines: Electric: float switch under the sole

q: The technician opens the gas locker and shows you this. What do you ask for before you sign?
a: A full spare bottle and the locker drain cleared
o: A full spare bottle; the drain can wait for the base
The drain cleared; you will buy a bottle in town
A note on the form that the locker holds water
why: Gas is heavier than air: the locker must drain overboard, not into the boat; and a half bottle with no spare runs out mid-week.

fig.title: Gas locker, cockpit
lines: Locker drain: blocked, 2 cm of water

q: Tuesday evening at anchor: there is a smell of gas in the galley. What do you do first?
a: Shut the valve at the bottle, ventilate, no flames or switches until the smell is gone
o: Switch on the fan and the lights to look for the leak at the stove
Light a burner to burn off the gas left in the pipe and hose
Pump the bilge and open the gas valve fully to flush the line
why: Gas sinks into the bilge: isolate at the bottle, ventilate, no sparks; then find the leak with soapy water on the joints.

fig.title: Galley, 19:30
lines: Smell of gas by the stove
Stove: off, gas valve at the bottle: open

q: In the galley you find this. The technician says the alarm 'kept going off, so we disconnected it'. What do you do?
a: Ask for it reconnected and tested before departure
o: Accept it; the solenoid switch is your safety
Sign and plug it in yourself later
Note it and rely on your nose for the week
why: A gas alarm that trips may be finding a real leak; it goes back on and is tested, and the leak is looked for, before you sign.

fig.title: Gas alarm
lines: Sensor: in the bilge under the stove
Solenoid switch at the stove: works

q: First evening in the marina, your crew start cooking. The stove swings on its gimbals as soon as a pan goes on. What do you tell them?
a: Lock the gimbals in harbour; free them only at sea so the pan stays level
o: Free the gimbals at all times; that is what they are for
Lock the gimbals at sea; free them in harbour
Wedge the stove with a cloth; the lock is for the oven
why: Gimbals keep the pan level when the boat heels; in a flat harbour the lock stops the stove tipping when someone leans on it.

q: After a night of rain the cockpit looks like this. What do you ask for before you leave the base?
a: The cockpit drains and the anchor-locker drain cleared and shown to run free
o: A bucket; you will bail the cockpit after rain
The scuppers checked; cockpit water drains over the sole
The anchor locker pumped out and the lid taped shut
why: A cockpit that does not drain fills in a sea; a blocked anchor-locker drain puts the water in the forepeak. Both are cleared at the base.

fig.title: Cockpit, Sunday 08:00
lines: Anchor locker: half full of water

q: You take over the catamaran with this. How do you plan the week's water?
a: Fill at every marina and make water only at sea, in clean water; 600 l will not last the week
o: Rely on the watermaker; run it every morning while in the marina
Fill once at the base; 600 l is plenty for 8 people for a week
Shower ashore only and never touch the watermaker all week
why: 600 l is under 11 l a day each for 8 people; a watermaker sucks oil and sewage in a harbour — it runs offshore in clean water.

q: Your crew are filling tank 1 from the pontoon hose. You look over the side and see this. What do you tell them?
a: Stop — that is the tank vent, so the tank is full
o: Carry on — that is the bilge pump clearing hose water
Carry on — the tank spills there until the air is out
Stop — a pipe has burst, call the technician
why: The tank breathes through a vent in the hull; water out of the vent means the tank is full — close that filler and move to the next tank.

fig.title: Filling tank 1
lines: Hose in the deck filler, 6 min
Water spurting from a small hull fitting
Starboard side, below the side deck

q: Wednesday, 07:30. Your crew call you to the aft shower. You check the panel. What do you do?
a: Switch the pump off, turn the selector to tank 2, then switch it on again
o: Leave the pump on; it draws from tank 2 by itself when 1 is empty
Switch the pump off and wait an hour for the gauge to recover
Open every tap with the pump running to bleed the air out
why: A pump running dry overheats and wears out; switch it off, change tanks, then let it prime with one tap open.

q: After the engine test you lift the aft bunk with the technician and find this. What do you ask for?
a: The valve checked before you leave and the fault noted on the form
o: The valve's outlet plugged so the bilge stays dry
Nothing — a relief valve is meant to let water out
The water heater switched off and taped for the week
why: A relief valve may drip as the water heats; a steady flow is a faulty valve or too much pressure — the base checks it, it is never plugged.

fig.title: Water heater, aft cabin
lines: Pool under the tank, draining to the bilge

q: Monday evening at anchor. The forward shower looks like this. What do you check first?
a: The shower-pump breaker, then the hair filter on the sump
o: The tank selector; the shower drains back to the tank
The heads seacocks; the shower drains through the toilet
The water-heater switch; the pump runs only with it on
why: A shower tray drains to a sump with its own pump, breaker and filter; hair clogs the filter and a tray left full floods the cabin sole.

fig.title: Forward shower
lines: Tray full, water over the sill
Drain button pressed: no pump noise

q: At check-in you pump the forward heads yourself. This is what you see. What do you do?
a: Ask for the joker valve to be changed and the heads tried again
o: Sign — set the lever to 'dry' after use and it stops
Sign; pump a few more strokes each time it is used
Note it on the form and keep the inlet seacock closed
why: Waste flowing back from the outlet is a worn joker valve, a cheap part the base changes in minutes — not a week of backflow.

fig.title: Forward heads
lines: A minute later: half full again
Brown water, from the outlet side

q: Wednesday in the Göcek bays, the holding tank is three-quarters full. You read the briefing notes again. What do you do?
a: Pump out at a station or a pump-out boat and get the card stamped
o: Open the valve after dark, when the patrol boats have gone
Motor three miles out of the bay and open the valve there
Lock the heads and use the beach toilets until Friday
why: In Turkey the blue card records each pump-out; the tank is emptied at a station and the card shows it was, not over the side.

fig.title: Briefing notes, Turkey
lines: Blue card: stamped at each pump-out
Pump-out boats and stations in the bays

q: Tuesday, 22:00. A crew member calls you to the aft heads. What do you do?
a: Stop pressing, switch its breaker off and use the other heads
o: Keep pressing in short bursts until the blockage clears
Pour boiling water into the bowl and press again
Turn the Y-valve to overboard to take the load off
why: A humming macerator is jammed; pressed on, the motor burns out. Breaker off, then the jam is cleared — not more pressing.

fig.title: Aft heads, electric
lines: Button pressed: motor hums, nothing moves

q: Going round the seacocks with the technician, you find this one. What do you do?
a: Leave it and ask the base to free or service it before you leave
o: Lever it with the winch handle; a seacock has to turn
Leave it open; it is only the sink and stays open anyway
Spray it with oil and try it again on Monday
why: A seized seacock forced with a lever can snap off below the waterline; the base frees or services it before you sign for the boat.

fig.title: Galley sink seacock
lines: Lever: will not move by hand

q: Monday at anchor there is water in the bilge again. You run this test. Where is it coming from?
a: A leak on the pressure side of the fresh-water system
o: The stern gland, dripping since you motored in
Rain through the deck fittings during the night
The holding tank, spilling over through its vent
why: Fresh water that comes only with the pump on is a pressurised pipe or joint; switch the pump off and trace the hoses from it.

fig.title: Bilge, Monday 08:00
lines: Pump off overnight: bilge stayed dry
Pump on: a trickle starts again

q: The technician says the gas 'has no leaks'. The regulator has a gauge. How do you check it yourself?
a: Open the bottle, close it again and watch the gauge hold for minutes
o: Light a burner and look for a steady blue flame
Smell along the pipe from the locker to the stove
Open the bottle and check the gas alarm stays silent
why: With every burner off, a sound system holds its pressure; a falling gauge is a leak — then soapy water on the joints finds it.

fig.title: Gas locker
lines: Bottle · regulator with a pressure gauge
Pipe to the galley: through a sealed gland

q: You find this in the gas locker. What do you ask for before you sign?
a: A new hose fitted before you leave
o: The cracks taped and noted on the form
A note on the form; you will check it daily
Nothing — the gas alarm will warn of a leak
why: Gas hoses perish with age and sun and carry a printed date; a cracked one is changed at the base, not watched for a week.

fig.title: Gas locker
lines: Rubber hose, regulator to the pipe

q: Monday, 12:30 in a bay. Your crew can't get the stove to light. You find this. What do you do?
a: Switch the red GAS switch on, then light the burner
o: Change to the spare bottle; this one has run out
Turn the burner knob harder to open the valve
Call the base; the regulator has failed
why: A solenoid valve at the locker opens only while its switch is on; it is the first thing to check when no gas reaches the stove.

fig.title: Galley, 12:30
lines: Burner: clicks, no gas, no smell

q: Tuesday afternoon, back from the beach, the fridge is warm. You find this. What do you do?
a: Open the fridge cooling seacock and check its pump runs
o: Switch the fridge off for an hour to let it reset
Turn the thermostat to maximum and keep the lid shut
Run the engine; the fridge is cooled by its water
why: A water-cooled fridge needs its seacock open; when you close the seacocks to go ashore, reopening this one belongs in the routine.

fig.title: Fridge
lines: Compressor running, hot to the touch
Seacocks: all closed when you went ashore

q: A 36 ft boat, six crew. After Sunday's swim the gauge already reads this. What rule do you set?
a: A short rinse after swims, wash up in seawater, drink bottled
o: Transom shower only, as long as each person likes
Carry on; half a tank lasts six people three days
Switch the pump off at night and carry on as usual
why: 75 l for six people for three days is about 4 l each a day, and the transom shower draws from the same tank at litres a minute.

lines: One tank, 150 l, full on Saturday

q: Sunday night in the town marina, your crew suggest this. What do you answer?
a: No — fill the tanks now, then take the hose out and close the filler
o: Yes, if the tap is only open a quarter turn
Yes — the tank vent spills anything extra over the side
Yes, if someone gets up at midnight to check the hose
why: A hose left on keeps pushing water in; a split pipe or a stuck vent puts the town's supply into the bilge while you sleep.

fig.title: The crew's plan
lines: Leave the marina hose in the filler

q: Tuesday at the town quay a neighbour points at your hull. You find this. What do you do?
a: Stop using the heads: the tank is full; get it pumped out
o: Nothing — it is the shower sump pump clearing
Close the heads seacocks; one of them is leaking
Open the holding tank's deck cap so the tank breathes
why: The holding tank vents through the hull; waste out of the vent means the tank is full — empty it before the heads are used again.

fig.title: Starboard side, by the heads
lines: Heads used all day, valve to 'tank'

q: Looking for the bucket in the cockpit, you find this. What do you ask the base?
a: Where the spare goes, upright, in a locker that drains overboard
o: Nothing — it is full and its valve is shut tight
For it to be wedged upright in that locker
For it to be stowed below, out of the hot sun
why: A bottle can leak at the valve; gas is heavier than air and runs into the bilge — spares stay upright in a locker that drains overboard.

fig.title: Port cockpit locker
lines: Spare gas bottle, full, on its side
Locker floor: open to the bilge
Gas locker: room for one bottle only

q: With a torch under the heads basin you find this. What do you ask for before you sign?
a: Two sound stainless clips on the hose before you leave
o: A note on the form; you will watch it all week
Nothing — you can close the seacock if it leaks
Tape round the clip to hold it until Friday
why: A hose below the waterline is held by two good clips; a rusted one can let go at sea and flood the boat — a five-minute fix at the base.

fig.title: Heads outlet seacock
lines: Hose on the tail: one clip
Clip: rusted through on one side

q: 42 ft catamaran. The technician lifts one floor panel and says 'bilges dry'. What do you ask?
a: To see every compartment of both hulls and each hull's pump run
o: Nothing — the two hulls share one bilge under the saloon
To see the starboard middle one; the ends stay dry
For 'bilges dry' on the form, signed by him
why: Each hull is its own bilge, often in several compartments with their own pumps; one dry panel says nothing about the other five.

fig.title: Catamaran bilges
lines: A bilge pump in each hull

q: Your crew have cooked their first supper aboard and ask how to turn the gas off. What do you show them?
a: Close the valve at the bottle, let the flame die, then close the knob
o: Close the stove knob; the bottle valve is closed in the morning
Close the stove knob; the bottle valve is only for leaving
Close the stove knob first, then the valve at the bottle
why: Shutting the bottle first lets the flame burn the gas left in the pipe, so no gas sits in the line between meals.

q: Your crew try the oven on Saturday evening. This is what happens. What do you tell them?
a: Hold the knob in for 10–15 seconds after it lights, then let go
o: Note it on the form: the oven's gas valve is faulty
Keep relighting it; it stays lit once the oven is warm
Wedge the knob in so the gas keeps flowing
why: The flame-failure device shuts the gas until its sensor is hot; hold the knob in until it is, and never jam it in.

fig.title: Oven
lines: Knob pushed in and turned, lit
Flame dies as soon as the knob is let go

q: Before going ashore you go to close these. Which position means closed?
a: The lever across the pipe, a quarter turn
o: The lever in line with the pipe, as it is now
The lever pointing down, towards the hull
The lever turned round twice, clockwise
why: A ball-valve seacock is open with the lever in line with the pipe and closed with it across — a quarter turn.

fig.title: Heads seacocks, under the basin
lines: Inlet: lever in line with the hose
Outlet: lever in line with the hose

q: Your crew ask whether they can drink the water from the galley tap. What do you tell them?
a: Drink bottled water; tank water is for washing and for boiling
o: Yes — the base fills the tanks from the town supply
Yes, once it has run for a minute to clear the pipe
Only from tank 1; tank 2 is for the showers
why: Tanks and hoses are not kept to drinking standard and the source varies; boiled tank water is fine for cooking, bottled is for drinking.

q: Your crew are washing up in a clear bay and ask whether the sink water goes to the holding tank. What do you answer?
a: No — sink and shower water go over the side; use little soap
o: Yes — everything that drains below goes to the holding tank
No — it drains to the bilge and the bilge pump clears it
Yes — so it does not matter how much soap they use
why: On most charter boats only the toilets feed the holding tank; grey water drains straight into the bay you swim in.

q: Tuesday, 18:00 at the town quay, the forward heads will not pump and you learn this. What do you do?
a: Stop pumping, close its seacocks, use the aft heads and call the base
o: Force the handle down hard to push the blockage through
Use it gently until Friday and tell the base at check-out
Call the base and ask them to send someone at their cost
why: Forcing a blocked pump breaks it; isolate it, call the base for where to get it cleared, and expect the charge — the blockage is the crew's.

fig.title: Forward heads
lines: Handle: stiff, will not go down

q: Thursday in a village harbour near Trogir: the gas runs out and there is no spare aboard. The shop has this. What do you do?
a: Call the base for where your type is swapped; eat cold or ashore till then
o: Buy it and fit your regulator with tape and a hose clip
Buy it and a camping stove to use on the saloon table
Buy it with the shop's own regulator and fit that one
why: Bottle valves differ by brand and country; a gas fitting is never adapted. The base knows where its bottles are swapped.

fig.title: Village shop
lines: Gas bottles: one brand, other valve
Your regulator: does not fit it
Shopkeeper: 'tape and a clip will do'

q: Thursday, 21:00 at anchor, wind forecast to rise in the night. You notice this. What do you do now?
a: Check each seacock, hose and the stern gland now, and call the base
o: Leave it; the pump keeps up, and you look at first light
Switch the bilge pump to manual to save the battery
Close every seacock, the engine's too, and wait for morning
why: Salt water that keeps coming is a seacock, hose, gland or rudder seal; find it now, with light and the base on the phone, not at 02:00 in F6.

q: Thursday, 07:00 in a bay. You will beat 15 miles back to the base in F5–6, heeled hard. You go below. What do you set?
a: Heads and sink seacocks closed, gas off at the bottle, gimbals free
o: Seacocks open to drain, gas off at the bottle, gimbals locked
Heads and sink seacocks closed, gas on for tea, gimbals locked
Seacocks open, gas on at the bottle, gimbals free for the kettle
why: Heeled, a sink or toilet below the waterline floods back through an open seacock; gas is off when nobody cooks, and the stove swings free.

fig.title: Below, 07:00
lines: Heads and galley sink: low when heeled
Gas valve at the bottle: open
Stove gimbals: locked since the marina

q: Croatia, 42 ft catamaran, eight crew. You plan two nights in a national-park bay. Reading this on Sunday, what do you plan?
a: One night in the park, then out past the limit to empty the tanks
o: Two nights in the park; empty the tanks at dawn when it is quiet
Two nights; the tanks last two days if the crew are careful
Two nights; motor out on the second morning to empty them
why: Tanks that fill in a day are emptied daily; the park gets one night and the run past the limit comes before the tanks are full.

fig.title: Holding tanks
lines: Base: 'full in about a day with eight'

q: Monday evening on the catamaran, eight crew. The water is going faster than you planned. You find this. What do you change?
a: Set the heads to SEA flush and ask the crew for short showers
o: Leave the heads; no showers at all until the next marina
Set the heads to SEA flush; the showers do not matter
Switch the pressure pump off between meals, nothing else
why: Fresh-water flushing on four heads takes tens of litres a day; sea-water flushing and short showers make 400 l last to the marina.
